l15-q01.answer: Epistemic: what the model does not know yet
options: Epistemic: what the model does not know yet
Aleatoric: the scatter between specimens of the same mix
Both shrink equally with more data
Neither; uncertainty is a property of the model family

l15-q02.answer: No model can predict better than about 5.0 MPa: that scatter is aleatoric
options: No model can predict better than about 5.0 MPa: that scatter is aleatoric
A model with enough capacity can bring its error below 5.0 MPa
The test set needs more mixes before the error can be trusted
The specimens were mislabeled, and the replicates should be removed

l15-q03.answer: The spread measures only epistemic uncertainty, and misses the scatter between specimens
options: The spread measures only epistemic uncertainty, and misses the scatter between specimens
Five networks are too few; fifty would cover 95%
The networks were overfitted, so their mean is wrong
The test mixes were outside the training range

l15-q04.answer: The calibration and test points are exchangeable: drawn the same way from the same population
options: The calibration and test points are exchangeable: drawn the same way from the same population
The model's errors are Gaussian
The model is a Gaussian process
The calibration set has at least 1,000 points

l15-q05.answer: The fraction of test points whose interval contains the true value
options: The fraction of test points whose interval contains the true value
The average width of the intervals
The probability the model's mean is within 1 MPa of the truth
The fraction of training points used to calibrate the interval

l15-q06.answer: A coverage check on mixes like the ones the search will reach; on the strongest mixes coverage fell to between 70% and 89%
options: A coverage check on mixes like the ones the search will reach; on the strongest mixes coverage fell to between 70% and 89%
A larger random split; 95% on 195 points is not significant
A second surrogate, to average the two intervals
Nothing: a calibrated interval stays calibrated everywhere

l15-q07.answer: A probabilistic surrogate of the evaluations so far, whose mean and uncertainty feed an acquisition function
options: A probabilistic surrogate of the evaluations so far, whose mean and uncertainty feed an acquisition function
A gradient of the objective, estimated by finite differences
A grid over the design space, refined around the best point
A model of the measurement noise only

l15-q08.answer: Both are random; one run of either could be luck
options: Both are random; one run of either could be luck
The emulator gives a different answer each time it is called
Thirty runs make the optimizer converge faster
Each seed tests a different design variable

l15-q09.answer: 91.6 MPa is the emulator's prediction, ±18 MPa, far from any tested mix; the next step is to cast and test it
options: 91.6 MPa is the emulator's prediction, ±18 MPa, far from any tested mix; the next step is to cast and test it
Bayesian optimization cannot find mixes stronger than the training data
The optimizer needed more than 25 evaluations to be sure
Nothing; the emulator was fitted to all 1,030 rows

l15-q10.answer: When the mean is above the best so far, or the uncertainty is large, or both
options: When the mean is above the best so far, or the uncertainty is large, or both
Only when the mean is above the best value found so far
Only where the uncertainty is largest
Only at points that have not been evaluated before
Probability of improvement
Expected improvement
Upper confidence bound with κ = 3
Thompson sampling

l15-q12.answer: It weights uncertainty more, so it samples more where the GP is unsure: it explores
options: It weights uncertainty more, so it samples more where the GP is unsure: it explores
It weights the mean more, so it samples closer to the best point: it exploits
Nothing; κ only rescales the acquisition
It samples where the measurement noise is lowest

l15-q13.answer: It draws one random function from the GP posterior and evaluates where that draw is highest
options: It draws one random function from the GP posterior and evaluates where that draw is highest
It evaluates where the GP's standard deviation is largest
It evaluates where the GP's mean is highest
It samples a point uniformly at random

l15-q14.answer: A model that is accurate everywhere it will be used, with as few labels as possible
options: A model that is accurate everywhere it will be used, with as few labels as possible
The best point, found with fewer evaluations than BO
A calibrated interval on the training data
The point of largest measurement noise
Random labeling: 9.5 MPa against 12.7
Least-sure labeling: 9.5 MPa against 12.7
They were identical, since both used the same GP
Neither improved on the 20-row starting model

l15-q16.answer: The least-sure rows are extreme mixes and ages at the edges, not where the test mixes are
options: The least-sure rows are extreme mixes and ages at the edges, not where the test mixes are
The GP should be refitted less often
Uncertainty sampling only works with neural networks
The pool was too small to choose from

l15-q01.answer: You can only evaluate it: set the inputs, run it, read one noisy number
options: You can only evaluate it: set the inputs, run it, read one noisy number
It comes from a neural network whose weights nobody can inspect or interpret
Its formula is known, but it is too long to differentiate by hand in the lab
It returns several outputs at once, so no single one of them can be optimized

l15-q02.answer: It updates a belief about the unknown curve with every experiment, and decides on that belief
options: It updates a belief about the unknown curve with every experiment, and decides on that belief
It applies Bayes' rule to estimate the gradient of the yield from noisy finite differences
Its objective has to be a probability, such as a yield, so the method is named after Bayes
Thomas Bayes first used it to choose experiments, and the name stayed with the method

l15-q03.answer: Use a gradient-based method: evaluations are cheap, gradients exist, and there are too many inputs
options: Use a gradient-based method: evaluations are cheap, gradients exist, and there are too many inputs
Use BO: it searches globally, so it is always safer than a local gradient-based method
Use BO with a batch acquisition, so that it can run thousands of evaluations at once
Use random search: with that many weights, no surrogate model of the loss can help

l15-q04.answer: Each gradient costs experiments, and the noise swamps the small differences on the flat cold side
options: Each gradient costs experiments, and the noise swamps the small differences on the flat cold side
The yield surface has many local optima, and L-BFGS-B was trapped in the nearest of them
L-BFGS-B needs exact second derivatives, which a noisy experiment can never provide
The temperature bounds stopped every step before it could get near the optimum

l15-q05.answer: Fit the GP to all data, maximize the acquisition, run that experiment, add it to the data
options: Fit the GP to all data, maximize the acquisition, run that experiment, add it to the data
Maximize the acquisition, fit the GP to the newest point only, run it, discard the older data
Run a batch of random experiments, fit the GP once, and report the maximum of its mean
Fit the GP, run the experiment where its mean is highest, then refit the acquisition function

l15-q06.answer: Exploration: the GP was still unsure there, so the acquisition paid for a look
options: Exploration: the GP was still unsure there, so the acquisition paid for a look
Exploitation: the GP mean predicted its highest yield of all at the hot end
A bug: expected improvement should never pick a point on the edge of the bounds
Chance: optimize_acqf returned one of its random candidates instead of the best

l15-q07.answer: It keeps sampling next to the best point so far, and can sit on a local optimum forever
options: It keeps sampling next to the best point so far, and can sit on a local optimum forever
It samples wherever the band is widest, and spends the whole budget learning the curve
It needs the gradient of the objective, which a laboratory experiment cannot provide
It can only use the GP's standard deviation, and has to ignore the mean altogether

l15-q08.answer: It weights uncertainty more, so it samples more where the GP is unsure: it explores
options: It weights uncertainty more, so it samples more where the GP is unsure: it explores
It weights the mean more, so it samples closer to the best point so far: it exploits
Nothing changes, because κ only rescales the acquisition and not its maximizer
It samples where the measurement noise is lowest, because κ divides the noise

l15-q09.answer: The second term, σφ(z): it grows where the GP is uncertain
options: The second term, σφ(z): it grows where the GP is uncertain
The first term, (μ − f*)Φ(z): it grows where the GP mean is high above the incumbent
Neither term: EI only exploits, which is the reason UCB was invented afterwards
Both terms equally: splitting EI into two terms is only algebra, with no meaning

l15-q10.answer: It scores only the chance of beating the best, not by how much
options: It scores only the chance of beating the best, not by how much
It uses the GP's standard deviation but ignores the GP's mean completely
It is computed by sampling, so its value is too noisy near the incumbent
Its margin ξ is negative by default, which pulls it toward the incumbent

l15-q11.answer: Zero: no uncertainty there, and no improvement to expect
options: Zero: no uncertainty there, and no improvement to expect
Its maximum, because the GP is most confident at a measured point
The measured yield itself, because the GP passes through the data
A negative number, which is how the loop avoids repeating experiments

l15-q12.answer: Far from the data, EI and its gradient underflow to zero, and the search stalls
options: Far from the data, EI and its gradient underflow to zero, and the search stalls
Taking the log moves the maximizer, so that the loop explores more than plain EI does
BoTorch can only minimize, so the acquisition has to be turned negative with a log
The log turns EI into a probability that sums to one over all the candidate inputs

l15-q13.answer: Draws from the posterior agree where the GP is sure and differ where it is not
options: Draws from the posterior agree where the GP is sure and differ where it is not
It alternates strictly: one exploring experiment, then one exploiting experiment
It draws a new value of κ at random each step and then maximizes the UCB with it
It picks a temperature uniformly at random and keeps it only if EI there is positive

l15-q14.answer: Temperature to [0, 1], yields to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so the kernel defaults fit
options: Temperature to [0, 1], yields to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so the kernel defaults fit
Without the two transforms the GP is only an approximation, and with them it becomes exact
The transforms remove the measurement noise from the yields before the GP is fitted
LogExpectedImprovement accepts inputs only between 0 and 1, so the transforms are required

options: It searches the acquisition, a cheap formula from the GP; the experiment runs once per pass
BoTorch estimates gradients of the yield itself from the experiments it has already run
It is not fine, and it is the reason BO only works on smooth, noise-free objectives
The gradients come from the Arrhenius formula inside the run_experiment function

options: Several seeds and a baseline: BO is random, and one run proves nothing
A larger budget: BO results can only be trusted after many dozens of experiments
